opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't say it doesn't matter at all; I'd say it matters much less than people think. Turing completeness is a statement about what a model can compute *in principle*, given unbounded time and memory and the right setting of its parameters. In practice none of those conditions hold. We have finite compute, finite memory, finite data, and above all we have to *learn* the program; nobody hands it to us.

So the real question in machine learning isn't "can this architecture represent the function?" Almost everything interesting can, in some technical sense. Even a single hidden-layer network is a universal approximator. The question is whether you can find that function efficiently from the data you actually have, and whether it generalizes. A Turing-complete model that needs an astronomical number of examples, or whose loss landscape makes the right solution essentially unreachable by gradient descent, is no better in practice than a much weaker model. Often it's worse, because more expressiveness means more ways to overfit.

You can see this with recurrent networks. People proved RNNs are Turing complete decades ago, but that proof relies on things like infinite-precision weights and carefully hand-constructed parameters. Train an LSTM with SGD and it will not learn to simulate an arbitrary Turing machine. The proof tells you about the space of possible solutions, not about the solutions learning will actually find. The same goes for the debates about whether transformers are Turing complete with or without chain of thought, and so on. It's intellectually interesting, but it doesn't tell you much about what these systems will do on real problems.

What does matter is inductive bias: what the model finds *easy* to learn, what it prefers when the data underdetermines the answer. That's where the real action is. Learning is fundamentally about making the right assumptions so that you can generalize from limited data. This is one reason I've long argued we need to unify the different paradigms, symbolic, connectionist, Bayesian, analogical, evolutionary. Each of them has a different inductive bias that makes certain kinds of structure easy to learn. A logic-based learner can pick up a recursive rule from a handful of examples, where a neural network might need millions and still not get it quite right, even though both are "universal" in the theoretical sense.

So my view is that Turing completeness is a kind of necessary sanity check at best. It tells you you're not ruling something out entirely. But the interesting differences between learning systems are all in the efficiency: computational efficiency, statistical efficiency, and how well their biases match the structure of the world. Those are the things that determine whether a system works, and Turing completeness is silent on all of them.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, because Turing completeness is a statement about what you can compute given unbounded resources, and nobody has unbounded resources. It tells you what's representable in the limit, not what's learnable or efficient. People love to point out that transformers aren't Turing complete, or that recurrent nets are, as if that settles something. It settles nothing. A lookup table with enough entries can approximate any function too, and that doesn't make it a good learning algorithm.

What actually matters is three things: what can you represent compactly, what can you learn from a reasonable amount of data, and what can you compute in a reasonable amount of time. Those are all finite questions, and Turing completeness is silent on every one of them. You can have two Turing-complete formalisms where one needs ten lines and the other needs ten million to express the same thing, and the ten-million-line one is useless in practice even though in principle it's equivalent.

And remember, in machine learning the hard part is not expressiveness. It's generalization. The more expressive your model class, the more data you need to pin down the right hypothesis, so maximal expressiveness is often the wrong goal. The whole game is finding the right bias, the right assumptions, so that the things you care about are easy to express and easy to learn, and the things you don't care about are hard or impossible. That's why I spent so much time on Markov logic, which is deliberately not Turing complete in the usual sense, but it's expressive enough to capture what people actually want to model, and tractable enough that you can do inference and learning. Turing completeness is a nice theoretical property to mention in a paper, but if you're trying to build something that works, it's close to the last thing I'd worry about.

astra-6.text:
Well, Turing completeness matters in principle, but it tells you very little about what you can do in practice. It says that, given enough time and memory, a system can compute any computable function. It doesn’t say how much time or memory you need, or how easy it is to get the system to do it.

Two programming languages can both be Turing complete, and yet writing a particular program in one can be vastly easier than writing it in the other. They have the same computational universality, but very different practical usefulness.

And in machine learning there’s an additional issue: can you learn the program? Showing that a model can represent a solution doesn’t show that your learning algorithm will find it, with the data and computation you actually have. So the interesting questions are about efficiency, learnability, and inductive bias. Turing completeness by itself doesn’t answer those questions.

sol-6.1.text:
Because Turing completeness tells you what a system can compute in principle, given unlimited time and memory. In practice, what matters is what it can learn and execute with the resources you actually have. Two systems can both be Turing complete and still differ enormously in how easily they solve a particular problem.

Take a conventional computer: it’s Turing complete, but that doesn’t give you the program you need. You still have to write it. With a learning system, the corresponding question is whether it can discover the right program from the available data. Saying that it can represent that program doesn’t establish that it can learn it.

So the interesting questions are about computational cost, sample complexity, and inductive bias. What problems does the architecture make easy to learn? What does it make difficult? Turing completeness, by itself, tells you very little about those things.
